title: Firebase Studio Alternatives: What to Use Instead
summary: Firebase Studio alternatives for the March 2027 shutdown: where your code, Firebase backend, App Hosting URL and dev.nix go, compared across 10 tools.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Firebase Studio shuts down on March 22, 2027 and deletes whatever is left in it, but Cloud Firestore, Authentication and App Hosting keep running, so only your workspace has to move.
- Both successors Google names can keep your published app's address: AI Studio through GitHub and App Hosting, Antigravity by deploying to your existing App Hosting URL.
- None of the 10 tools here runs your` .idx/dev.nix` file, and only Replit, GitHub Codespaces (through a dev container feature) and Coder document Nix, so the package list moves by hand.
- Eight of the nine tools after ours have a $0 way in, though Coder's runs on hardware you pay for; Google Cloud Workstations has no free tier, and neither do we.


If you're weighing Firebase Studio alternatives, you're working to a date. Google announced the sunset on March 19, 2026. New signups and workspaces ended on June 22, 2026, and the shutdown follows on March 22, 2027, when any remaining data "is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered."


Your Firebase backend isn't part of that deletion, so the question is where your code and workspace setup land. We checked every price on November 13, 2026, about four months before the shutdown.


[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) heads the list as our own product, though it can't import a Firebase project or Nix file, so read its cons first. Next are the two tools Google's migration page names: Google AI Studio, then Google Antigravity. Code-view replacements follow, ranked by how directly their docs let you carry a Nix-defined environment, then app builders, ranked by what their docs say about an existing Firebase project.


## What shuts down in March 2027, and what keeps running


Firebase Studio was a browser workspace built on Code OSS, running "a full virtual machine (VM) powered by Google Cloud", configured through a Nix file at` .idx/dev.nix` , with Gemini agents on top. It was free, with 3 workspaces per user by default.


Google's migration page is plain about the scope: "This sunset only applies to the Firebase Studio development environment." Cloud Firestore, Authentication and App Hosting "will continue to work outside of Firebase Studio".


That distinction tripped people up, judging by one anecdotal Reddit thread. In r/Firebase's[Firebase Studio Is Shutting Down](https://www.reddit.com/r/Firebase/comments/1rysgyk/firebase_studio_is_shutting_down_what_you_need_to/) , several commenters asked whether Firestore, Auth, Functions and` firebase_admin` would stop too.


If you also run Gemini in your terminal, our[Gemini CLI alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/gemini-cli-alternatives) roundup covers that side.


## The best Firebase Studio alternatives, side by side


The last column answers the question for anyone who opened Firebase Studio on several machines: where does the replacement run? Pricing shows any free way in, then the cheapest paid plan at its month-to-month price.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Only Antigravity needs a local install, for its free tier and Google's Firebase export. Every other row opens in a browser, though Coder and Cloud Workstations need someone to set them up first.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** A cloud workspace on any device


**Overview:** If you'll miss opening the same workspace from any machine, that's where we overlap with Firebase Studio. Each Awesomic project gets a dedicated cloud computer with up to 1 TB of storage, and agents install, run and ship real programs on it: a website, an internal CRM or a dev environment.


Work there doesn't stop when you log off. You can open it in a browser, in our iOS and Android apps, or in a desktop app on macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (x64) and Linux.


Where the Prototyper gave you Gemini, you pick the agent: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or OpenCode, with models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI. We're backed by Y Combinator.


**Key features:**


- Parallel agents, one chat per agent, all working on the same project files.
- One bill for every model, or bring a Claude or Codex plan you already pay for.
- One-click publishing, and project sharing by link.
- Connections to GitHub, Slack and Notion, plus your own MCP servers.


**Pricing:** On agentic plans, Light runs $19 per person each month, Basic $99, Pro $199 and Studio $499, and each price doubles as that person's AI budget. Billing is monthly, with no refunds, and leftover budget doesn't carry over.


For a person to do the rebuild, start on a separate expert plan instead: a Dedicated expert, quoted on a call, for a code rebuild, or All-in-One, listed at $3,219 a month, for a no-code one. Each includes one Light subscription.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** A cloud computer per project, desktop and mobile apps, four agents on one bill, sessions that keep going while you're signed out


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Zip and download your workspace, plus` /home/user/.idx/ai` if you want the chat history.
2. Push the code to a GitHub repo.
3. Start on Pro, open a project and connect GitHub.
4. Paste the package list from` .idx/dev.nix` into a chat and ask an agent to install it.
5. Run the app and, once it works, publish it with one click.


**Why it's a good Firebase Studio alternative:** You keep a cloud workspace that opens anywhere, without depending on one model family.


**Final verdict:** Pick us if the any-device workspace mattered more than Firebase wiring. If your app lives on Firebase, AI Studio or Antigravity is the better pick, since both can keep your App Hosting URL.


To try it on your own project,[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Pro.


### 2. Google AI Studio


**Overview:** Google steers Prototyper users here, and anyone who prefers the browser. In Firebase Studio, clicking "Move now", "Prepare for AI Studio", then "Move to Google AI Studio" opens your code in a new AI Studio workspace.


Build mode runs a full-stack environment with a Node.js runtime, producing "standard apps running in a Cloud Run container". It can provision Firestore and Firebase Authentication, and it builds React and Node.js web apps or native Android apps in Kotlin.


Publishing has two routes. Option A keeps your` *.hosted.app` URL: put the` .env` Gemini key into the App Hosting backend, usually named` studio` , then connect it to a GitHub repo created from AI Studio. Option B publishes to Cloud Run at a new` *.run.app` address, which you must add under Authorized domains for Google Sign-In.


**Key features:**


- A direct import from Firebase Studio.
- Two-way GitHub sync, including existing repos, with a conflict dialog.
- A browser emulator for Android projects.


**Pricing:** Google says AI Studio costs nothing to use in every region where it's offered, and Google AI Pro raises the limits for $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year. On the Starter Tier, eligible accounts can have up to 2 full-stack apps published with no billing account; beyond that, Cloud Run usage is billed.


**Pros:** Google's own import path, keeps your App Hosting URL, free to use


**Cons:** No real-time collaborative editing, web or Android projects only, with no documented terminal workspace, the Starter Tier excludes Workspace accounts and past paid Cloud billing accounts


**What survives the move:** Your code, your Firebase project and, through Option A, the URL your users already know.


**Final verdict:** Choose AI Studio if you built with the Prototyper and want the shortest route to keeping your live app where it is.


### 3. Google Antigravity


**Overview:** Antigravity is Google's pick if you mostly used Code view, started from a template or imported repo, or outgrew the Prototyper. Its migration guide promises the familiar interface of VS Code "running locally on your hardware", and Pro and Ultra plans add Remote Agents, which run in a Google-managed environment you open from a browser.


To migrate, you'll need Node.js 20 or newer and Firebase CLI 15.10.0 or newer. Use "Zip and Download", open the folder in Antigravity and prompt` @fbs-to-agy-export` , or run` npx firebase-tools@latest studio:export` . Then "Publish my app" has the agent run` firebase deploy` , which goes to your existing URL if you'd published to App Hosting.


**Key features:**


- An export command that writes` .firebaserc` and` firebase.json` for you.
- The Firebase Emulator Suite running on your own machine.
- An optional Firebase MCP server for the agent.


**Pricing:** Individuals pay $0 with "Basic weekly rate limits", Google AI Pro is $19.99 monthly or $199.99 yearly, and Ultra starts at $99.99 a month. Business access runs through Gemini Enterprise, from $30 per seat per month or pay-as-you-go with no seat fee.


**Pros:** Deploys to your current App Hosting URL, a free tier, Google's guided export


**Cons:** The free tier and the Firebase export run only on your own machine, Remote Agents need paid Pro or Ultra, Google's models page says Claude 4.6 and GPT-OSS leave on November 18, 2026, and lists Claude 5.5 for paid Pro, no bring-your-own-key for extra limits


**Best reason to move here:** Your Firebase project, CLI and emulators all keep working, now on your own machine.


**Final verdict:** Pick Antigravity if you lived in Code view and don't need to open your workspace from someone else's computer.


### 4. Replit


**Overview:** Replit is the only tool here whose docs put Nix under every app, as Firebase Studio did. Each app runs in a cloud workspace you open in the browser, configured with` .replit` and` replit.nix` , because "Replit uses Nix to manage packages and environments".


Your` dev.nix` still doesn't drop in: Replit imports from ZIP, GitHub and several builders, with no Firebase Studio importer or Firebase guide. Its own database is PostgreSQL-compatible, so your Firestore wiring stays your job.


**Key features:**


- Agent in Free, Power and Max modes, with Free Mode on Starter, Core and Pro.
- Pro adds up to 15 collaborators and database rollback up to 28 days.
- A Design Canvas, and up to 5 builders on Core.


**Pricing:** Core includes $20 of credit "towards more powerful models" and costs $20 a month, or $18 if you pay annually, while Pro costs $100, or $90 a month on annual billing. A free Starter plan exists, but its one published app "will automatically go down after 30 days".


**Pros:** Nix as the environment layer, a browser workspace you can open anywhere, imports from Bolt and Lovable


**Cons:** No Firebase or Firebase Studio import docs, publishing is billed by usage, Full build, connectors and AI Integrations need Core


**The Nix advantage:** Packages from your` dev.nix` have an obvious home in` replit.nix` , even if you copy them across yourself.


**Final verdict:** Choose Replit if you want a cloud workspace close to Firebase Studio's design and don't mind rewiring the backend.


### 5. GitHub Codespaces


**Overview:** Codespaces gives you a cloud VM of 2 to 32 cores, configured by a` devcontainer.json` in your repo and opened in the browser or desktop VS Code. For a Code-view user, that's close to Firebase Studio's editor and terminal.


Nix comes through an official add-on: the dev container feature` ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/nix:1` installs Nix and takes an "Optional comma separated list of Nix packages". You paste in the packages from your` dev.nix` yourself, since nothing reads the old file, and GitHub's docs offer no Firebase guidance.


**Key features:**


- Prebuilds, so a codespace opens with dependencies already installed.
- Environment settings kept in the repo with the code.
- An export of unsaved work to a branch when usage is blocked.


**Pricing:** GitHub Free accounts get 120 core hours and 15 GB-month of storage a month, about 60 hours on a 2-core machine, and GitHub Pro gets 180 and 20. Past that, compute runs $0.18 an hour on 2 cores up to $2.88 on 32, plus $0.07 per GB-month of storage.


**Pros:** A monthly free quota, Nix through an official feature, your repo stays the source of truth


**Cons:** Storage bills while a codespace exists, even stopped, organization plans get no free quota, hosting the finished app isn't included


**What makes it a Firebase Studio alternative:** A browser VM with a terminal is back, defined in your own repo.


**Final verdict:** Pick Codespaces if your project is already a GitHub repo and you want the editor back in a browser tab.


### 6. Coder


**Overview:** Coder runs cloud workspaces on infrastructure you own, so there's no hosted service to lose. Environments are templates or dev containers kept as code, opened in VS Code, JetBrains, Cursor or Jupyter, and Claude Code, Codex and Cursor agents can run inside them.


Like Codespaces, Coder handles Nix through an official add-on, but its Nix(OS) module is still early access. It builds a project's dev shell from a Nix flake in your repo, so your` dev.nix` packages move into a flake you write. We found no Coder docs on Firebase.


**Key features:**


- Workspace templates you keep in version control.
- Autostart and autostop schedules to cut idle compute.
- Web and desktop IDE connections.


**Pricing:** Community is free and lets you "Provision unlimited self-hosted workspaces on the infrastructure you already own". Premium is billed annually per user at a price Coder doesn't publish, and AI Premium is custom.


**Pros:** A free self-hosted tier, no hosted service that can shut down, an official Nix module


**Cons:** You install and operate it with no hosted option on the pricing page, Premium pricing needs a demo, audit logging, quotas and multi-org access control are Premium only


**What owning it buys:** Your workspaces sit on infrastructure you control, so no vendor holds them or can set a date to delete them.


**Final verdict:** Pick Coder if you have people to run infrastructure and want the team's workspaces on machines you control.


### 7. Google Cloud Workstations


**Overview:** Where Firebase Studio's docs describe the VM it runs, they link to Cloud Workstations, a managed VM product you run in your own Google Cloud project. Workstations open in a browser or a local IDE.


Environments are "defined as containers, which you can extend, modify, or even fully replace", with no Nix guide, so your` dev.nix` packages go into a container image. The editor is Code OSS for Cloud Workstations, the base Firebase Studio used, with JetBrains IDEs and Posit Workbench as options.


**Key features:**


- VPC Service Controls, Cloud Audit Logs and IAM access rules.
- Auto-stop after a set time without activity.
- Several IDEs on one managed platform.


**Pricing:** You pay Compute Engine and disk at normal rates, plus $0.05 per vCPU per hour while a workstation runs and $0.20 per cluster per hour whether or not anyone uses it. Google's example of one developer on e2-standard-4 for 198 hours with 100 GB comes to $217.36 a month, $144 of it the cluster fee.


**Pros:** The same Code OSS base, runs in your own cloud account, enterprise access controls


**Cons:** Needs a billed Google Cloud project and an admin to set up clusters, the cluster fee runs even when idle, its built-in assistant needs a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise subscription, which Google stopped selling on October 9, 2026


**The VM Google's docs point to:** You run that product yourself, minus Firebase Studio's free tier.


**Final verdict:** Choose Cloud Workstations if your company already runs on Google Cloud and wants developer VMs under its own controls.


### 8. FlutterFlow


**Overview:** Firebase Studio had Flutter templates and Android emulator previews, and FlutterFlow is where those projects fit best. FlutterFlow Studio's docs explain how to "Connect an existing Firebase project manually", so your Firestore data and Auth users stay where they are. The newer prompt-based FlutterFlow has no Firebase docs.


The catch is the code: we found no FlutterFlow doc for importing existing code, so even a Flutter template app gets rebuilt in Studio's visual editor. You build in the browser or the FlutterFlow Studio desktop app.


**Key features:**


- Firebase integration and Cloud Functions on every Studio plan.
- One build for both the App Store and Google Play.
- Plugins for Codex and Claude Code.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 but has no code download or APK, and Basic is $39 a month, or $29 billed yearly. Pro is $80, or $60 yearly, and Max is $150, or $113 yearly, with one subscription covering FlutterFlow and FlutterFlow Studio.


**Pros:** Connects to the Firebase project you already have, native mobile builds, a free plan to test


**Cons:** Flutter only; in Studio, no code download on Free and GitHub push needs Pro; the prompt-based FlutterFlow can't export source or push to GitHub


**For Flutter template users:** Your backend stays on Firebase while you rebuild the app in an editor made for Flutter.


**Final verdict:** Choose FlutterFlow if your Firebase Studio project was a Flutter app and the Firebase backend should stay untouched.


### 9. Bolt.new


**Overview:** Bolt.new runs a prompt-to-app loop like the Prototyper's, with the project running inside the tab in Chromium browsers. In Safari, its docs say, "Previews are hosted rather than running in the browser".


Its help center has no Firebase page, it ships its own Bolt Cloud database with Supabase as an option, and "Bolt only supports JavaScript-based backends, so languages such as PHP or Python aren't compatible". That rules out projects built on Firebase Studio's Go, Java, .NET or Python Flask templates.


**Key features:**


- GitHub import and sync for an exported project.
- Imports from Figma and Google Stitch.
- Expo support for mobile apps.


**Pricing:** Free is $0 with 300K tokens a day and 1M a month, and Pro is $25 a month billed monthly, starting at 10M tokens with rollover. Teams costs $30 per member per month, and yearly billing saves up to 28%.


**Pros:** A prompt-to-app loop in the browser, GitHub sync, a free plan


**Cons:** JavaScript backends only, no Firebase docs, Code view, visual edits and the database are desktop-only


**When it beats the Prototyper:** Its database is built in, so a prompt-built app needs no Firebase account.


**Final verdict:** Pick Bolt.new if you built a JavaScript prototype and are happy to rewire or replace its Firebase backend.


### 10. Lovable


**Overview:** Lovable suits the Prototyper user who wants out of Firebase as well as Firebase Studio. Its import doc says "Lovable migrates the code and moves your database and users to Lovable's built-in backend".


The same doc notes that "The code export does not contain your database records or your app's user accounts", so plan how those move before you switch. Its only Firebase doc covers Cloud Messaging for push notifications.


**Key features:**


- Project import from a ZIP of up to 250 MB.
- Git sync with GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket on all plans.
- Built-in hosting on` lovable.app` domains.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 with no credit card and 5` lovable.app` domains, and Pro costs $25 a month, or $250 a year, with 100 monthly credits and custom domains. Business is $50 a month and adds SSO and role-based access.


**Pros:** One place for code, data and hosting, Git sync on every plan, a documented import path


**Cons:** Web apps only, the free plan can't edit or download code in Lovable, though Git sync still copies it to GitHub, every message after the import spends credits


**If you're done with Firebase:** It's the one tool here that documents moving users and a database onto its own backend, though its guide covers other builders, not Firebase.


**Final verdict:** Choose Lovable if you'd rather leave the Firebase backend behind than keep running it.


## Moving out: what carries over and what stays behind


Google's three routes start from the "Move now" button, and this table follows each piece of a Firebase Studio project through them.


What you have To Google AI Studio To Google Antigravity Anywhere else


Your code Opens in a new AI Studio workspace Zip and Download, then` @fbs-to-agy-export` or` studio:export` Zip and Download


Firestore, Auth, App Hosting Keep running Keep running; export writes` .firebaserc` and` firebase.json` Keep running; the wiring is yours


Your` *.hosted.app` URL Kept with Option A; Option B gives a new` *.run.app` URL Kept when the agent deploys to App Hosting Kept by linking` firebase init apphosting` to the` studio` backend; other hosts give a new URL


` .idx/dev.nix` Not mentioned in Google's steps Ignored in` firebase.json` ; cleanup offers to delete it Copy the package list by hand


Agent chat history Not stated; save` /home/user/.idx/ai` first Not in the zip; zip that folder separately Not in the zip; zip that folder separately


Shared workspaces Only the creator can use "Move now" Same Same; others duplicate the workspace or zip it manually


Two rows catch people: chat history isn't in the zip, though Prototyper prompts also sit in your` git log` , and only the workspace's creator can press "Move now".


Exports can stall too, so Google suggests deleting` node_modules` , large media, build folders and a bulky` .git` first. In that earlier r/Firebase thread, one commenter said "Move now" to AI Studio "kept failing" and the Antigravity export reported "too much traffic", so start early.


If nobody on your team has hours to rebuild after the export, our comparison of[unlimited web development vs freelancers](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/unlimited-web-development-vs-freelancers-ship-3x-faster) weighs two ways to buy that time.


## Your dev.nix file has no automatic new home


Google's migration page never mentions` .idx/dev.nix` , and the Antigravity export goes further. Its cleanup step tells the agent to "Ask the developer if they'd like to remove the .idx/dev.nix file. Most times this file will be unused but the developer may have added some configurations that they'd like to keep", and the` firebase.json` it writes ignores` .idx` . No Google path documents running your Nix config.


That only hurts if you lose the package list, because a Nix-declared environment travels well. In their ICSE 2024 paper on[reproducible build environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.00424) , Malka, Zacchiroli and Zimmermann rebuilt "14 452 out of the 14 461 jobs" from a six-year-old Nixpkgs revision, a 99.94% success rate. Their study covers Nixpkgs packages rebuilt with Nix, not Firebase Studio's file, so the lesson is strongest where Nix still runs: keep the list.


To carry it over:


- Copy` .idx/dev.nix` into your repo before exporting, and decline if the cleanup step offers to delete it.
- On Replit, move the package names into` replit.nix` .
- On Codespaces, add the Nix feature to` devcontainer.json` with the same packages.
- On Coder, put them in a Nix flake for its early-access Nix module.
- Anywhere else, install them through a container image or package manager, then run the app to see what's missing.


If Replit's metered publishing puts you off, our[Replit alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/replit-alternatives) guide compares builders that bill differently.


## Don't swap one shutdown for another


Firebase Studio "launched as a preview", in Google's words, and previews can end. It isn't the only cloud workspace to announce its end this year: Ona, formerly Gitpod, announced on October 13, 2026 that "we joined OpenAI to take that work further with Codex" and shut Ona Cloud on October 31.


The worry is old. In a 2016 Journal of Cloud Computing study on[vendor lock-in](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13677-016-0054-z) , Opara-Martins, Sahandi and Tian found that "as many as 71% of the participants claimed vendor lock-in risks will deter" their organizations from adopting more cloud services. That was 114 UK respondents, but two shutdown announcements in seven months make it feel current.


The defense is keeping your code somewhere you control. AI Studio, Bolt.new and Lovable sync with GitHub, FlutterFlow Studio pushes to it on Pro, Codespaces starts from your repo, and Antigravity keeps the code on your machine. The same advice applies to us: our Subscription Terms let you download your files for 30 days after canceling, but a GitHub copy doesn't run out.


## How to choose by what you used Firebase Studio for


One question narrows these Firebase Studio alternatives fast: did you build with the App Prototyping agent, or work in Code view?


### If you built with the App Prototyping agent


Start with Google AI Studio. It's Google's pick for Prototyper users, the import starts inside Firebase Studio, and Option A keeps your live URL while Firestore and Auth stay put.


To leave Firebase entirely, Lovable documents moving a database and users onto its own backend from other builders, though not from Firebase. Bolt.new suits JavaScript prototypes, but with no Firebase guide in its docs, the backend is yours to rewire or replace.


### If you worked in Code view


Antigravity is Google's answer, but its migration path runs on your own machine. From another device you can use Remote Control, which needs your computer left on, or Remote Agents on a paid Pro or Ultra plan. In an r/Firebase thread asking[what the alternative is](https://www.reddit.com/r/Firebase/comments/1sst2up/with_firebase_studio_shutting_down_in_a_year/) , the poster said they liked editing and showing projects "if I'm not in front of my computer".


That's one Reddit user, who also found AI Studio prompt-first, a complaint that has dated: its Code tab now allows direct edits. If the browser matters, Codespaces and Replit give you a full workspace in a tab and a home for your Nix packages.


A Flutter template project fits FlutterFlow Studio, which connects to the same Firebase project. Teams that want workspaces on infrastructure they control should try Coder, and teams already on Google Cloud, Cloud Workstations. For a local AI editor that isn't Google's, our[Windsurf alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/windsurf-alternatives) roundup covers more.


## Firebase Studio competitors we left off


Two Firebase Studio competitors missed the cut. Google Cloud Shell is free for Google Cloud users, with 5 GB of persistent home storage on a temporary VM, but it would have been a fourth Google product.


v0, which runs in the browser and deploys to Vercel, lost its slot to Bolt.new and Lovable, and our[Lovable alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/lovable-alternatives) guide reviews it.


## What to do before March 22, 2027


This week, zip every workspace you care about, keep the` /home/user/.idx/ai` folder for chat history, and copy` .idx/dev.nix` into your repo. Then move one small project through your chosen route and check that the App Hosting URL still answers before moving the rest.


If the rebuild is more than your team can absorb, we can match you with a[design engineer who builds](https://www.awesomic.com/design-engineer) the new setup, on our Dedicated expert plan.


## FAQ


### When does Firebase Studio shut down?


On March 22, 2027, when all remaining data is permanently deleted. Signups and new workspaces stopped on June 22, 2026, and you can work in and migrate existing workspaces until then.


### Will my Firestore database and users stop working?


No. Google says Firestore, Auth and App Hosting keep working outside Firebase Studio, because the sunset covers only the development environment, so your published app keeps running while you move the code.


### Can I keep my hosted.app URL after moving?


Yes, on three routes. AI Studio's Option A connects a GitHub repo to your existing App Hosting backend, Antigravity's "Publish my app" deploys to the URL you already have, and anywhere else you can run` firebase init apphosting` and link the` studio` backend.


### Is there a free Firebase Studio alternative?


Several. Google AI Studio is free to use, Antigravity has a $0 individual tier, GitHub Free includes 120 Codespaces core hours a month, and Replit, FlutterFlow, Bolt.new and Lovable have free plans with limits. Coder Community is free if you supply the servers.


### Is there a Firebase Studio alternative for Flutter apps?


FlutterFlow Studio is the closest fit, because it connects to an existing Firebase project and builds for the App Store and Google Play. If its visual editor isn't for you, our[FlutterFlow competitors](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/flutterflow-competitors) roundup weighs other Flutter builders.
